action_criteria.expected_evidence: Four Rascovsky features from the informant history and examination (disinhibition, loss of empathy, stereotyped routines, executive-predominant profile) with functional decline
action_criteria.label: Structured informant history and bedside cognitive screen scored against the Rascovsky features
action_criteria.rationale: The diagnosis of bvFTD rests on the behavioural features obtained from an informant; here they must be separated from what Parkinson's disease and its treatment explain.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Executive and social-cognition deficits disproportionate to psychomotor slowing, with preserved recognition memory and visuospatial function
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery including executive and social-cognition measures
action_criteria.rationale: Quantifies the executive and social-cognition profile and the relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function, which separates bvFTD from PD-related cognitive impairment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, chemistry, liver tests, thyroid function, B12, folate and inflammatory markers
action_criteria.label: Reversible-cause blood tests: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, ESR, CRP
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory contributors before attributing decline to neurodegeneration.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Moderate bifrontal and mild anterior temporal atrophy with preserved hippocampi, posterior cortex and midbrain
action_criteria.label: MRI brain without contrast, dementia protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Shows the frontal and anterior temporal atrophy pattern, looks for midbrain atrophy of PSP and excludes structural and vascular causes.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe frontal and moderate anterior temporal hypometabolism or hypoperfusion with normal posterior cingulate, parietal and occipital cortex
action_criteria.label: FDG-PET when the structural picture is unresolved
action_criteria.rationale: Frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism with posterior sparing supports FTD over PD dementia, DLB and AD; perfusion SPECT is the substitute.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reduced putaminal dopamine transporter uptake, left greater than right
action_criteria.label: DaTscan only for the separate question of the co-existing parkinsonian disorder
action_criteria.rationale: A presynaptic dopaminergic deficit supports the clinical PD diagnosis; it does not diagnose FTD or separate PD from other degenerative parkinsonism.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansion; no GRN or MAPT variant
action_criteria.label: Genetic counselling and FTD gene panel (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT)
action_criteria.rationale: Onset in his late forties with parkinsonism, and a father with parkinsonism and late cognitive decline, make a familial FTD gene possible; testing follows counselling.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General criteria and genetics evidence only
action_criteria.label: Literature on FTD with parkinsonism (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the criteria and on familial FTD; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.

Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; never use haloperidol, risperidone or other strong dopamine D2 antagonists, which worsen parkinsonism.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state which features are present, the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible or probable).
Explain why Parkinson's disease (PD-MCI or PD dementia) does not account for the early social and behavioural syndrome with frontal atrophy and preserved posterior cortex.
Review dopaminergic therapy as a contributor to the impulsive spending and sexual disinhibition: keep levodopa at the lowest effective dose for his motor symptoms and do not add a dopamine agonist.
Address safety and capacity: driving, finances (impulsive spending, protection of assets, lasting power of attorney) and his capacity in the ongoing litigation.
Arrange caregiver education and support for his wife, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.
Offer genetic counselling before any genetic test, and discuss what a result would mean for his son and other relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, with co-existing Parkinson's disease

differential.diagnosis: Parkinson's disease dementia or PD-MCI as the sole explanation
differential.key_features: For: established, levodopa-responsive PD. Against: early disinhibition, loss of empathy and stereotyped routines with mild motor disease, a frontal executive and social-cognition profile, frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with preserved posterior cortex.

For: impulsive spending and sexual disinhibition on levodopa. Against: levodopa monotherapy at a moderate dose, never an agonist; loss of empathy, rigid routines, executive dysfunction and frontal atrophy are not explained by it.
Against: no visual hallucinations, dream enactment or fluctuations; preserved visuospatial function and posterior cortex.
Against: full vertical saccades, asymmetric levodopa-responsive parkinsonism with rest tremor, no early falls, no midbrain atrophy.
Against: preserved recognition memory, visuospatial function, hippocampi and posterior cortex.
Raised by parkinsonism with behavioural change before 50. Against: onset at 48 with typical asymmetric levodopa-responsive PD and normal liver tests; ceruloplasmin and copper settle it if obtained.

key_clinical_evidence: Four Rascovsky features (disinhibition, loss of empathy, stereotyped routines, executive-predominant profile) with loss of his job and bifrontal and anterior temporal atrophy meet probable bvFTD.
An early social and behavioural syndrome with mild motor disease, frontal atrophy and preserved posterior cortex and hippocampi does not fit PD-MCI or PD dementia.

Impulsive spending and sexual disinhibition on levodopa raise a dopaminergic impulse control disorder, but loss of empathy, rigid routines, executive dysfunction and frontal atrophy are not explained by it.
Onset before 65 and a father with parkinsonism and late cognitive decline support offering genetic counselling; C9orf72 expansions can present with parkinsonism.

clinical_assessment.impression: 4 of the 6 Rascovsky features are present on informant history and examination (disinhibition, loss of empathy, stereotyped routines, executive-predominant profile), with documented decline in daily function. Apathy is not counted because it overlaps with Parkinson's disease and treated depression. This meets possible bvFTD; imaging and neuropsychological testing decide whether it is probable. Memory and visuospatial function are relatively preserved on the bedside screen.

results.finding: Three of six core features within the first three years define possible bvFTD.
Probable bvFTD requires functional decline and supportive imaging.
C9orf72, GRN and MAPT account for most familial FTD; parkinsonism occurs with each of them.

C9orf72-associated FTD with concurrent p.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. C9orf72 expansions and GRN and MAPT variants cause most familial FTD; counselling precedes any genetic test and any predictive testing of relatives. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle: probable bvFTD in a 52-year-old man with co-existing, levodopa-responsive Parkinson's disease, previously labelled PD-MCI. Teaching: an early social and behavioural syndrome with frontal atrophy and posterior sparing does not fit PD dementia; a dopaminergic impulse control disorder is the drug mimic; DaTscan answers only the parkinsonism question. The optional FTD gene panel finds a C9orf72 expansion, which would make the diagnosis definite; cholinesterase inhibitors, used in PD dementia, are not recommended in FTD.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. N is a 52-year-old investment banker, terminated 20 months ago, who has been followed by a general neurologist for Parkinson's disease (diagnosed 4 years ago, mild right-sided onset). He was referred to the cognitive neurology clinic after his primary neurologist expressed concern that the cognitive and behavioral changes 'don't fit the expected pattern for PD-MCI.' He was initially diagnosed with PD-MCI by a prior neurologist 2 years ago and has been managed with carbidopa/levodopa with good motor response. His wife of 2 years — he married her during the period of behavioral changes — is the primary informant. She describes behaviors that preceded their marriage and were not apparent to her at the time: he made several large, impulsive financial decisions shortly before they met that his family has since described to her as completely uncharacteristic. He spent $180,000 on a collection of vintage motorcycles within 6 months, despite having no prior interest in motorcycles. He was terminated from his bank position for 'performance and conduct issues' — he had made unauthorized client fund transfers and made multiple sexually inappropriate comments to a junior colleague. He denied all of these events and filed an unsuccessful wrongful termination suit. He is now in a persistent legal battle over a disputed real estate transaction he initiated. At home, he has a highly rigid routine — he eats the same three items for breakfast in identical order each day and becomes enraged if the sequence is altered. He has stopped reading financial news, which was his lifelong obsession. He has no insight into any of these behaviors. His motor PD symptoms have remained mild and respond well to levodopa; he has taken carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg three times daily since diagnosis and has never been prescribed a dopamine agonist or an MAO-B inhibitor. His father has Parkinson's disease and advanced cognitive impairment (in a memory care facility at age 82). His adult son from his first marriage reports that he showed no concern when the son was hospitalised last year and did not visit or call. His wife reports no visual hallucinations, no acting out of dreams and no day-to-day fluctuation in alertness.

neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral palmomental reflexes. No fasciculations, no muscle wasting and no tongue atrophy. No myoclonus.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mild right-sided slowing and imprecision of rapid alternating movements, in keeping with bradykinesia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal except subtly reduced blink rate. Full vertical and horizontal saccades; no supranuclear gaze palsy.
neurological_exam.gait: Right-sided Parkinsonian gait — reduced right arm swing, mild right-sided shuffle. Left arm swing preserved. Normal stride length. No festination.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Shows flat affect. MoCA 21/30: executive tasks severely impaired (trails 0/1, letter fluency — 5 F-words), memory (3/5 delayed recall), attention 5/6. He describes his bank termination as 'politics' and his prior neurologist's MCI diagnosis as 'overreaction.' Prominent anosognosia.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild right-sided rest tremor (4 Hz). Mild cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist. Mild right-sided bradykinesia; on the left, mild finger-tap slowing only. No alien hand phenomenon. Bulk normal, no fasciculations. Strength 5/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric. No Babinski. No Hoffmann sign.
